description_ru: Пари на пятьдесят евро превращается в Камино: жёлтые стрелки, новые друзья, туман над Монте-до-Гозо и слёзы перед собором.
text:
Let me begin with a confession: I did not walk the Camino de Santiago for spiritual reasons. I walked it because a colleague, in a moment of weakness at a leaving party, bet me fifty euros that I could not manage a hundred kilometres on foot. I like to think that most of the pilgrims who have trudged towards the tomb of Saint James over the past thousand years had nobler motives. But the road, I discovered, is remarkably undemanding about why you came.

The most popular final section begins in Sarria, a modest town in the Spanish region of Galicia, about a hundred and fifteen kilometres from the cathedral at Santiago de Compostela. The sum is not accidental. To receive the official certificate, called the Compostela, a walker must cover at least the last hundred kilometres, and have the pilgrim's passport stamped twice a day along the way. I bought my credencial in a café, filled in my details, and acquired, at the same time, a small scallop shell to tie on my rucksack. The shell, an ancient emblem of the pilgrimage, was apparently useful for scooping water in the Middle Ages. Mine was mainly decorative, and promptly swung into my kneecap.

Navigating is almost insultingly simple. Yellow arrows, painted on trees, walls, bollards and the occasional unwilling cow, point the way, and concrete waymarkers, topped with a stylised shell, count down the remaining distance. On the first morning, I saw the one marked 111 and felt a surge of confidence. By the fortieth waymarker, I was less sure of that confidence's foundation. My feet, long accustomed to office carpets, had begun to file complaints, in writing, with each step.

Yet the landscape was extraordinary. Galicia is green in a way that suggests it has been supplied with a private rain service, which in fact it has. The path wound through eucalyptus groves, between stone walls furred with moss, along lanes that smelled of cut grass and woodsmoke and, now and then, cows. Tiny villages with names like Portomarín and Palas de Rei appeared at intervals, each with a Romanesque church, a bar, and a smiling woman who would sell you a coffee and a slice of tortilla for suspiciously little. At every stage, the daily rhythm was the same: rise at dawn, walk, eat, walk some more, arrive, shower, sleep. Nobody checks your email in a eucalyptus grove, and the absence of that small, constant itch becomes a luxury more precious than any hotel. It is a form of life so simple that it feels, after a few days, like an unusually effective kind of medicine.

The people were the greatest surprise. Within two days, I had acquired a loose, shifting tribe. There was Henrik, a Danish dentist who talked about nothing but his dog. There was a retired French teacher called Odile, who recited poetry as she walked and did not hold with complaining. There were three students from Seoul, a lively, ironic Brazilian nurse, and an American man in his seventies who was walking in memory of his wife and had a way of saying "well, we're here" that I found unbearably moving. Henrik's dog, whom we never met, acquired in our imaginations a personality of rare complexity. We would overtake and be overtaken, meet again at a bar, share a bench and a bag of olives, and part, never certain whether we would see each other again. Strangely, we usually did.

A conversation on the road follows its own odd rules. People begin by comparing blisters, as strangers always do, and within an hour they are telling you about divorces, doubts, and the books they never wrote. It is as though the exertion strips away the usual armour. Nobody can seem important with a sunburnt nose and a plaster on each heel. I told Odile, over a plate of octopus, that I had no idea why I was there. "Nobody does," she replied. "The road tells you later. It is slow, but it is quite honest."

On the final morning, the path rose through pine woods to the hill of Monte do Gozo, the Mount of Joy, from which medieval pilgrims got their first glimpse of the cathedral spires. It was shrouded in fog, naturally. We descended into the suburbs of Santiago, which are depressingly like every other suburb, then through narrow, echoing lanes, beneath an arch, and into the Praza do Obradoiro, the great square in front of the cathedral. And there it was, a baroque cliff of grey stone, wet with rain and glowing in the weak light.

I had been warned that the arrival would be emotional, and I had scoffed. Then I saw the American, sitting alone on the flagstones with his rucksack, quietly crying, and the Danish dentist put an arm around him without a word, and I discovered that I was perfectly capable of scoffing and weeping at the same time. We collected our certificates, and we attended the pilgrims' mass, during which, on a lucky day, eight men swing a giant silver censer, the botafumeiro, through the transept on a rope, so that it hurtles overhead trailing a comet of incense. It is magnificent and slightly alarming, much like the whole enterprise.

I won the bet, of course. My colleague paid up with a very good grace and asked, a little wistfully, whether the road was hard. I told him it was, but that the difficult part was not the walking. The difficult part was going home, and finding that nobody else had noticed that the arrows had not stopped.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: undeˈmanding, exˈertion, Romanˈesque. В Romanesque главное ударение на последнем слоге.
«w»: губы округляются и вытягиваются вперёд, как при «у»: walk, weakness. Не «в».
Окончание -ing с носовым «ŋ» (morning, walking): язык не отрывается от мягкого нёба, «г» не слышно.
Дифтонг «eɪ» растягивается: «е» + «и»: waymarkers, stage. Не краткое «э».

questions.question: Why did the writer walk the Camino?
questions.answer: Because a colleague bet him fifty euros he could not walk a hundred kilometres.

questions.question: What must a walker do to receive the Compostela?
questions.answer: Walk at least the last hundred kilometres and collect two stamps a day.

questions.question: What is the botafumeiro?
questions.answer: A giant silver censer swung through the cathedral transept.

questions.question: Why was going home the hardest part?
questions.answer: Nobody else had noticed that the arrows had not stopped.
